legacy_report:
SOURCE: "InterCode: Standardizing and Benchmarking Interactive Coding with Execution Feedback", John Yang, Akshara Prabhakar, Karthik Narasimhan, Shunyu Yao (Princeton). Venue as printed on p1: "37th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2023) Track on Datasets and Benchmarks." arXiv:2306.14898v3, 30 Oct 2023.

COVERAGE: 29 of 29 pages, 106,622 of 106,622 chars (text extracted with page markers). References (pp10-13) skimmed for origins. Everything else read in full: main text, appendices A-C, Tables 1-14 and the prompt templates.

CLAIMS (ranked by importance for verification loops)

- claim: Every model does better with multi-turn execution feedback ("Try Again") than with a single turn on SQL. GPT-4 shows the largest gain.
  number: GPT-4 SQL 9.1 -> 73.7; gpt-3.5-turbo 10.5 -> 47.3
  setup: InterCode-SQL (Spider 1.0 dev, 1034 tasks, MySQL), zero-shot Single Turn vs Try Again with n = 10. Temperature 0. Observations capped at 1000 tokens.
  quote: "performance across different levels of task difficulty (SQL) and different file systems (Bash) is superior in the interactive setting for all models, with a notable multi-fold increase for GPT-4 (9.1% → 73.7%) on the InterCode-SQL task." Table 2 rows: "gpt-3.5-turbo 22.6 8.3 5.7 3.6 10.5 72.5 44.3 43.7 21.1 47.3" / "gpt-4 19.8 7.2 4.6 3.0 9.1 87.5 76.7 66.7 52.4 73.7"
  where: p7, Table 2 and text

- claim: The Bash gains are real but much smaller than the SQL gains.
  number: gpt-4 34.0 -> 48.5; gpt-3.5-turbo 34.5 -> 46.5; text-davinci-003 24.6 -> 38.7; chat-bison-001 17.7 -> 19.2
  setup: InterCode-Bash (200 NL2Bash-derived tasks across 4 file systems), Single Turn vs Try Again with n = 10
  quote: Table 3: "gpt-3.5-turbo 30.0 39.6 33.3 37.0 34.5 45.0 49.1 45.0 48.1 46.5" / "gpt-4 25.0 37.7 36.7 40.7 34.0 41.7 47.2 51.7 59.2 48.5" / "chat-bison-001 12.1 22.5 16.7 22.2 17.7 13.8 24.5 18.3 22.2 19.2"
  where: p7, Table 3

- CAVEAT ON THE ABOVE (important for the note): in Try Again, each observation includes the gold-derived reward. The episode also stops automatically once the reward hits 1. So the agent is checked against an oracle, not left to verify itself. ReAct and Plan & Solve stop when the agent judges it is done.
  quote: "This continues until a reward of 1 (task completion) is achieved or the number of turns (n) is exhausted." Template: "Output: <Observation from Intercode Environment> Reward: <Value ∈ [0, 1]>"; Fig 2: "The "Try Again" termination constraint is conditioned on reward = 1, while ReAct [51] and Plan & Solve [43] are determined by the agent itself."
  where: p6, p27 (Table 11), p6 Fig 2

- claim: Giving the full schema shrinks the single-turn vs interactive gap a lot, but interaction still comes out ahead.
  number: gpt-3.5-turbo 67.9 -> 72.8; text-bison-001 61.4 -> 63.9; chat-bison-001 49.2 -> 54.9
  setup: InterCode-SQL with the relevant DB schema added to the question, max 10 turns
  quote: "while Single Turn performance improves drastically, a non-trivial difference in favor of Try Again remains." Table 5: "gpt-3.5-turbo 90.7 70.2 59.2 37.3 67.9 92.7 74.9 67.2 43.4 72.8"
  where: p21, Table 5

- claim: Success rate rises with more turns, then plateaus. As history builds up, models repeat actions and ignore recent observations.
  number: none (Fig 3 curves only)
  setup: Try Again, all 7 models, Bash and SQL, turns 1-10
  quote: "both Figure 3 exhibits a plateauing in Success Rate and and Error %. This suggests that as the amount of context and feedback builds up, models are less capable of discerning relevant past history toward future actions. In late-turn scenarios, task episode trajectories often reveal repetition of earlier actions, a failure to effectively use recent observations towards deciding an appropriate next action, or an inability to recognize that a current problem-solving chain of thought is inconclusive or futile."
  where: p7, §5.1 "Failure cases"

- claim: On SQL, the error rate (non-admissible actions) falls sharply after turn 1 because models start discovering context. It does not keep improving in later turns. Bash shows no such early drop.
  number: SQL turn 1 90.2%, turn 2 46.4%; 60.3% of second-turn actions use SHOW TABLES/DESC
  setup: Try Again, GPT-3.5, per-turn Error %
  quote: "SQL 90.2 46.4 34.4 39.7 31.1 42.9 51.5 47.4 48.4 46.6" / "Bash 23.1 28.6 34.7 37.5 37.6 42.9 39.3 37.1 33.7 38.2"; "60.3% of second turn actions contain either the SHOW TABLES orDESC keywords"; "in later turns, the rate of admissible actions does not improve consistently... a model will tend to make small, cursory adjustments to the prior action based on execution feedback, often resulting in both a repetition of the same types of mistakes and hallucinations that introduce new issues."
  where: p21, Table 6 and text

- claim: Prompting strategy matters, and the best one depends on the task. ReAct is best on SQL. Try Again (which sees the reward) is best on Bash. Plan & Solve has a very high error rate on Bash.
  number: SQL SR: Try Again 47.3 / ReAct 58.7 / P&S 49.1. Bash SR: 46.5 / 20.5 / 28.0
  setup: gpt-3.5-turbo, full datasets; n = 10 for Try Again and ReAct
  quote: "SQL 47.3 7.25 46.4 58.7 5.30 6.94 49.1 4.29 16.2" / "Bash 46.5 6.15 24.9 20.5 4.40 20.4 28.0 6.65 53.3"; "explicit reasoning frameworks such as ReAct and Plan & Solve policies generally achieve higher success rates (SQL: 47.3% → 58.7%) with fewer turns and a higher rate of admissible commands."
  where: p8, Table 4

- claim: Plan & Solve is weak at "adjusting on the fly in response to execution feedback." ReAct and P&S solve largely different subsets of tasks.
  number: 57% (407/708) SQL; 27.6% (21/76) Bash overlap
  quote: "tasks solved by both strategies withgpt-3.5-turbo make up 57% (407/708) and 27.6% (21/76) of the union of all successfully solved InterCode-SQL and InterCode-Bash tasks respectively."
  where: p8

- claim: Adding a refine stage after Plan & Solve does not help much.
  number: SR 45.5, 6.34 turns, Error 22.4%, on 44 SQL tasks
  quote: "These preliminary tests have an average Success Rate of 45.5, a Number of Turns of 6.34 ... and an Error % of 22.4. Compared to the original Plan & Solve performance presented in Section 5.2, this strategy does not yield a significant improvement."
  where: p22, §B.3

- claim: Without a reasoning framework, models only correct errors and discover context. They do no other kind of reasoning.
  quote: "current language models do not demonstrate any innate reasoning capacity for the interactive coding task beyond error correction and context discovery."
  where: p23, §B.4

- claim: The Bash single-vs-interactive gap holds up under standard errors.
  number: gpt-4 38.37 ± 1.20 -> 52.70 ± 3.50; gpt-3.5-turbo 36.63 ± 1.83 -> 47.40 ± 1.23
  setup: file systems 2-4 only (FS1 is harder and was excluded)
  quote: "gpt-3.5-turbo 36.63 ± 1.83 47.40 ± 1.23" / "gpt-4 38.37 ± 1.20 52.70 ± 3.50"
  where: p22, Table 7

- claim: Humans (the authors) reach a higher success rate. They break queries into sub-problems, where agents write one monolithic command.
  number: 13/15, SR 0.87
  setup: 15 random SQL tasks, n = 10, human decides when to submit
  quote: "The human task worker was able to complete 13 of 15 tasks (Success Rate = 0.87) with low Error %"
  where: p25, §B.6

- claim: The reward is a graded score, but Success Rate counts only exact completion. Bash: R = 0.34·TF-IDF similarity of stdout + 0.33·(1 − erf(missed/extra file-system changes)) + 0.33·(fraction of shared paths with matching md5). SQL: IoU × rescaled Kendall τ.
  quote: "The scalar weights for each component are arbitrarily assigned."; "the scalar 3/7 output shown in the figure is treated as a 0 when quantifying whether the task was completed via the 0/1 Success Rate metric."
  where: p16, p19

LIMITS
- Main comparison: the Try Again agent sees a reward computed from the gold answer, and the episode stops on success. The single-turn vs interactive delta therefore measures oracle-guided retry. It does not measure unaided self-verification. The authors frame Try Again as probing "error correction from feedback" (p6 Fig 2).
- The prompting-strategy comparison uses only gpt-3.5-turbo. The B.3 refine experiment covers 44 tasks. The human baseline is 15 tasks, done by the authors themselves.
- Python (MBPP) has an environment but no results are reported.
- Authors concede that only Bash/SQL/Python are covered. The CTF dataset is internally inconsistent: §5.3 says "100 CTF objectives from picoCTF" (p9), while Limitations says "the CTF dataset is limited to just four task instances due to our manual curation procedure" (p9). The CTF demonstration is qualitative and needed a hint ("without the provided hint regarding the usefulness of the "sleuthkit" library, the agent fails", p24).
- Bash file system 1 was deliberately made harder (p16). Bash tasks number only 200.
- Dated: models are 2023-era (text-davinci-003, PaLM-2 bison, Vicuna-13B, StarChat-16B). Observations are truncated to 1000 tokens, and open-source models get max_new_tokens 100 (p20), which may handicap them.
- Suggested remedies for long-horizon degradation are speculative: "A larger context window size, retrieval of useful memory, and more adaptive reasoning paradigms" (p7).

BUILDS ON
ReAct (Yao et al., 2023 [51]); Plan-and-Solve (Wang et al., 2023 [43]); OpenAI Gym API (Brockman et al., 2016 [5]); Docker (Merkel, 2014 [34]); datasets NL2Bash (Lin et al., 2018 [32]), Spider (Yu et al., 2018 [55]), MBPP (Austin et al., 2021 [4]); picoCTF ([42]); "admissible" actions from Yao et al., 2020 [49]. Related execution-feedback work it cites: Self-Debug (Chen et al., 2023 [12]), Reflexion (Shinn et al., 2023 [40]), Execution-guided synthesis (Chen et al., 2018 [11]), REPL synthesis (Ellis et al., 2019 [17]), LEVER (Ni et al., 2023 [35]), Self-Edit (Zhang et al., 2023 [59]), compiler feedback (Wang et al., 2022 [44]).

CODE
- POMDP and metric definitions (p4): "We use the Success Rate (SR) metric, defined as the proportion of task episodes where r = 1. We also define the Error % metric, which is the percentage of non admissible actions across task episodes."
- Interactive loop (Fig 5, p15), verbatim:
  env = BashEnv(...)
  for # of episodes:
    env.reset()
    policy = ...
    done = false
    while not done:
      policy(obs) → act
      env.step(act)
        → obs, done
  env.close()
- Bash reset uses git (p15): "git status -s" for diffs and "git reset –hard; git clean -fd;" to restore state.

FIGURES
- Fig 3, p8: success rate vs number of interaction turns (1-10), per model, for Bash and SQL under Try Again. This shows the rise-then-plateau of more turns at a glance. Best candidate for the note.
- Fig 2, p6: the four prompting strategies (Single Turn, Try Again, ReAct, Plan & Solve) with their termination rules. It makes clear that Try Again stops on reward and the others stop on the agent's own judgement.
- Fig 1, p2: the agent-environment loop for Bash plus the evaluation (file-system diff, md5, lexical similarity). It shows execution-based verification of state, not just output.
- Table 9, p24 (a table, not a figure): Try Again and ReAct trajectories side by side on the same SQL task. Try Again keeps hallucinating column names. ReAct discovers context and submits. Good concrete illustration of the failure modes.
- Fig 4, p9: GPT-4 CTF trajectory, with feedback-to-next-action links highlighted.

PROBLEMS
- Extraction was clean. Tables were mostly parseable. Bold "best" markers were lost.
- The Vicuna row of Table 7 is split across a chunk boundary. Reconstructed as "16.73 ± 5.00 27.67 ± 4.15", which is low risk.
- Table 1's caption says "two environments with Bash and SQL" but the table lists three (Bash, SQL, Python). The CTF count is inconsistent (100 vs four).
- The Fig 8 SQL difficulty distribution is an image with no extractable values.
- No embedded instructions found.
